content: Efforts to educate prescribers and raise awareness among healthcare workers (HCWs), communities, and patients aim to reduce the demand for and over-prescription of injections. Improper collection and disposal of sharp waste pose significant risks to healthcare providers, waste handlers, and the community, as they may lead to injuries and the transmission of bloodborne infections. To address this, a new policy recommends procuring adequate quantities of safety boxes for the containment of safety-engineered devices. This issue will also be tackled through a global campaign and implementation plan tailored to specific country contexts. Unsafe injection practices can transmit bloodborne pathogens such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV to patients, often due to syringe reuse. Healthcare workers are primarily at risk of accidental needlestick injuries (NSIs). Reusing syringes to access multi-dose medication vials used for multiple patients can also spread viruses, bacteria, and other pathogens. These infections reduce the life expectancy and productivity of both patients and HCWs, while placing a financial burden on communities and healthcare systems due to avoidable treatment and opportunity costs. Data on the prevalence and treatment costs of HIV, HBV, and HCV, as well as their transmission through unsafe injections, highlight the significant disease burden caused by these practices. However, the risks extend beyond these three pathogens, including nosocomial bacterial infections, malaria, viral hemorrhagic fevers, muscle necrosis, and skin lesions such as cutaneous tuberculosis and granulomas. The World Health Organization (WHO), in collaboration with the Safe Injection Global Network (SIGN) and other international health organizations, has made substantial efforts since 2000 to address unsafe injection practices. WHO has developed a three-pillar strategy: The 1999 WHO policy recommended the exclusive use of auto-disable (AD) syringes for all immunization injections. Syringes with reuse prevention (RUP) features and sharps injury protection (SIP) mechanisms have been available since the 1990s and 2000s, respectively. While some models are cost-comparable to standard syringes, others are significantly more expensive, which can be a barrier for lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Safety-engineered syringes include various mechanisms to prevent reuse and needlestick injuries. For example, AD syringes have features that disable the plunger after a single use, while RUP syringes allow variable dosing and may include mechanisms to break the plunger if reuse is attempted. SIP syringes protect against needlestick injuries by covering or retracting the needle after use, either manually or automatically. To develop evidence-based recommendations, WHO employed the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. This method evaluates the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations. Evidence quality is categorized as high, moderate, low, or very low, based on factors such as risk of bias, consistency, and precision. Recommendations are classified as strong or conditional, either in favor of or against an intervention. A systematic review of the use of SIP and RUP syringes among HCWs delivering intramuscular, subcutaneous, or intradermal injections found moderate-quality evidence supporting their effectiveness in reducing NSIs. The benefits of these devices likely outweigh any potential risks, particularly in settings with high prevalence of bloodborne diseases. Preliminary cost-effectiveness analyses also support their use. WHO recommends the introduction of SIP syringes for HCWs, with the expectation that this will reduce NSI incidence and associated disease transmission. The guideline development process involved a multidisciplinary Guideline Development Group (GDG) and external experts. The GDG reviewed evidence, assessed the balance of benefits and harms, and developed recommendations through consensus. External experts provided valuable feedback, which was incorporated into the final guideline. In summary, WHO strongly advocates for the use of safety-engineered syringes, such as SIP and RUP devices, to enhance injection safety, protect HCWs and patients, and reduce the transmission of bloodborne infections. These recommendations are based on systematic evidence reviews, cost-effectiveness analyses, and global expert consensus.
